topics.title: India's mixed economy: private and public sectors

learn.hook: You may travel on a government-run train, pay with a private bank's app and buy a snack made by a cooperative, all in one trip. That is India's mixed economy.
points: India follows a mixed economy, in which the private sector and the public sector exist side by side.
Private sector: enterprises owned by individuals or groups of individuals, such as sole proprietorships, partnerships, Joint Hindu Family businesses, cooperatives and companies.
Public sector: enterprises owned, managed and controlled by the central government, a state government or both, either wholly or partly.
The government decides the role of each sector through its industrial policies; public enterprises can take the form of departmental undertakings, statutory corporations or government companies.

example.q: Classify: (a) Indian Railways, (b) a Pune software firm owned by two friends, (c) Steel Authority of India Limited.
steps: Indian Railways is run by the Ministry of Railways: public sector.
The software firm is owned by private individuals: private sector.
SAIL is owned mainly by the Government of India: public sector.

learn.reallife: India's skies show the mix too: airports are run by the public Airports Authority of India and also by private operators under concession agreements.

learn.hook: Indian Railways has its own minister in the Union Cabinet. That tells you how it is organised: as a department of the government.
points: Departmental undertakings are enterprises set up as departments of a ministry and are considered part of the government. Examples: Indian Railways, the Department of Posts, defence production units.

Features: funded by annual appropriations from the government's budget and revenue goes to the treasury; subject to the accounting and audit controls applicable to government activities; employees are government servants recruited under government rules; a part of the ministry with no separate legal entity; directly controlled by and accountable to the ministry.
Merits: effective control by Parliament; high degree of public accountability; revenue goes to the treasury; most suitable where national security or strategic control is involved.

Limitations: lack of flexibility; delays in decisions due to bureaucracy (red tape); undue political interference; civil servants may lack business experience; often insensitive to consumer needs; unable to take advantage of business opportunities.

example.q: The government wants an enterprise to make sensitive defence equipment under the direct watch of the ministry and Parliament. Which form suits it, and why?
steps: Strategic and security concerns need tight government control.
A departmental undertaking is directly under the ministry and accountable to Parliament.
example.answer: Departmental undertaking, because it allows close government control where national security is involved.

learn.reallife: India Post runs as a department of the Ministry of Communications, so major decisions on postal services pass through the ministry.

learn.hook: LIC was born on the pages of an Act passed by Parliament in 1956. That 'birth by statute' gives it a special mix of government power and business freedom.
points: Statutory corporations are public enterprises brought into existence by a Special Act of Parliament or a state legislature. The Act defines their powers, functions, rules, employees and relationship with government. Examples: Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC Act, 1956), Food Corporation of India (Food Corporations Act, 1964).
They are described as having the power of the government and the operational flexibility of private enterprise.

Features: set up under an Act; separate legal entity that can sue, be sued, own property and enter contracts; wholly owned by the state, with the government having ultimate financial responsibility; usually independently financed through borrowings from government or the public and revenue from sales; employees are not civil servants; not subject to the budget, accounting and audit procedures of government departments.

Merits: independence in functioning and high operational flexibility; government generally does not interfere in financial matters; framed by Parliament, so it has a clear legal framework; it can be a valuable instrument for economic development combining public interest with business efficiency.

Limitations: in practice, operational flexibility is limited and government or political interference in major decisions is common; where public money is involved, misuse and corruption may occur; any change in its constitution requires amending the Act by Parliament.

example.q: The government wants to set up a public enterprise with a clear legal identity, autonomy in finance and recruitment, but answerable to Parliament. Which form suits it?
steps: A clear legal identity and autonomy point to a separate legal entity with flexibility.
Accountability to Parliament comes from being created by a Special Act.
That combination is a statutory corporation.

learn.reallife: The Food Corporation of India, set up by a 1964 Act, buys grain from farmers and stores and distributes it across India for the public distribution system.

learn.hook: BHEL, SAIL and HAL all end with 'Limited'. They are companies like any other, except that the government holds the majority of their shares.
points: A government company is a company in which not less than 51% of the paid-up share capital is held by the central government, or by one or more state governments, or partly by the central government and partly by state governments. A subsidiary of a government company is also a government company. Examples: BHEL, SAIL, Hindustan Aeronautics Limited.

Features: registered under the Companies Act, 2013; separate legal entity that can sue, be sued and own property; management regulated by the Companies Act and its articles; employees appointed under the company's own rules; funds come from the government and other shareholders, and it can raise money from the capital market.
Merits: easy to establish (only Companies Act requirements); separate legal entity; autonomy in management decisions; can control the market and curb unhealthy business practices.

Limitations: where the government is the only shareholder, Companies Act provisions have little relevance; it evades constitutional responsibility because it is not directly answerable to Parliament like a department; management and administration rest with the government, which may interfere.

example.q: Of a company's paid-up capital of ₹100 crore, the central government holds ₹40 crore and a state government holds ₹15 crore. Is it a government company?
steps: Total government holding = 40 + 15 = ₹55 crore.
55% ≥ 51%, and central plus state holdings can be added.
example.answer: Yes, it is a government company (55% held by governments).

learn.reallife: Hindustan Aeronautics Limited, which builds the Tejas fighter, is a government company: registered under the Companies Act but majority-owned by the Government of India.

topics.title: Comparing the three forms of public enterprise

learn.hook: Department, corporation or company? A board-exam favourite: read the case, spot the clues, name the form.
points: Creation: departmental undertaking by a ministry (no separate law); statutory corporation by a Special Act; government company by registration under the Companies Act, 2013.
Legal entity: none for a department; separate entity for both corporation and company.
Finance: department from the budget; corporation from the government plus its own borrowings and revenue; company from government and private shareholders, and the capital market.

Employees: civil servants in a department; the corporation's own rules; the company's own rules. Accountability: department to the ministry; corporation to Parliament through the Act; company to its board and shareholders, with the government as main shareholder.
Clues for cases: 'part of the ministry', 'civil servants', 'budget' → department; 'Special Act', 'statute' → statutory corporation; 'Companies Act', '51% shares', 'Limited' → government company.

example.q: Case: 'XYZ was set up under a law passed by Parliament. It has its own employees, is not part of any ministry and can borrow from the public.' Identify the form.
steps: Created by a law passed by Parliament = Special Act.
Own employees and not part of a ministry = separate entity with autonomy.
So it is a statutory corporation.

learn.reallife: India uses all three: the Department of Posts (department), Food Corporation of India (statutory corporation) and Coal India Limited (government company).

topics.title: Changing role of the public sector

learn.hook: In the 1950s the government built steel plants itself. Today it sells shares in some public enterprises. Why the change?
points: Original role after Independence: development of infrastructure (heavy industry, power, transport); regional balance (setting up units in backward areas); economies of scale (in industries needing huge investment); check over concentration of economic power in a few private hands; import substitution (self-reliance by producing goods at home).
The New Industrial Policy of 1991 changed the approach to make public enterprises efficient and competitive.

Reduction in the number of industries reserved for the public sector, opening them to private firms; today only a couple of strategic areas, such as atomic energy and railway operations, remain reserved.
Disinvestment: selling part of the government's equity in public enterprises to private investors and the public, to improve efficiency and raise resources.

Policy on sick units: sick public enterprises were referred to the Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) to decide on revival or closure (BIFR was abolished in 2016; such cases now go to the National Company Law Tribunal under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016). Memorandum of Understanding (MoU): an agreement between the government and a public enterprise that gives management more autonomy while holding it accountable for agreed targets.

example.q: The government sells 10% of its shares in a profitable public enterprise through the stock exchange. Which post-1991 policy measure is this, and what does it aim at?
steps: Selling government-held shares to the public is disinvestment.
It aims to bring in private ownership and market discipline, improve efficiency and raise funds.
example.answer: Disinvestment, aimed at improving efficiency and raising resources.

learn.reallife: Steel plants at Bhilai, Rourkela and Durgapur were set up by the public sector partly to develop backward regions: the 'regional balance' role in action.

quiz.explain: Import substitution aimed at self-reliance.
steps: Making at home what was earlier imported.
That is import substitution, aimed at self-reliance.
Answer: import substitution

quiz.q: Under the 1991 policy, sick public sector units were referred to
options: the Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR)
quiz.explain: Under the 1991 policy, BIFR examined whether sick units should be revived or closed. (BIFR was abolished in 2016; the National Company Law Tribunal now handles such cases.)
steps: The 1991 policy sent sick public units to a board that decided revival or closure.
That board was BIFR (abolished in 2016; NCLT now handles such cases).
Answer: the Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR)

quiz.q: Why did the public sector take up industries like steel and heavy machinery after Independence?
options: They needed huge investment and gave economies of scale that private firms then could not provide

quiz.explain: Large capital needs and long gestation made public investment necessary.
steps: Steel and heavy machinery need huge investment.
They give economies of scale that private firms then could not provide.
Private firms were not banned from all industry.
Answer: They needed huge investment and gave economies of scale that private firms then could not provide

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The government reduced the number of industries reserved for the public sector after 1991. Reason (R): The 1991 policy aimed to open industries to private enterprise to increase efficiency and competition.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true; the aim of greater competition explains why reservations were cut.
steps: A: reserved industries were reduced after 1991 – true.
R: the policy aimed to open industries to private firms for efficiency and competition – true.
That aim is the reason reservations were cut.
So both are true and R correctly explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Misses the link between policy aim and measure

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Disinvestment increases the government's shareholding in public enterprises. Reason (R): Disinvestment was one of the measures of the 1991 industrial policy.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
A is true, but R is false
quiz.explain: A is false: disinvestment reduces government shareholding. R is true.
steps: A: disinvestment increases government shareholding – false; it reduces it.
R: disinvestment was a 1991 measure – true.
So A is false, but R is true.
Answer: A is false, but R is true

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why did the government first build so many factories and then start selling shares in them?'
teach.praise: Tweet! First to build infrastructure and balance regions, then after 1991 to make them efficient through disinvestment and MoUs!

revise.summary: After Independence the public sector built infrastructure, balanced regions, gained scale, checked concentration of power and replaced imports. Since 1991, reservations were cut and disinvestment, sick-unit reform and MoUs were introduced.

traps: Disinvestment reduces, not increases, government shareholding

learn.hook: The phone in your pocket may be designed in one country, assembled in another and sold in a hundred more. The firms that run such networks are global enterprises.
points: Global enterprises (multinational corporations, MNCs) are huge industrial organisations that extend their operations across many countries through branches, subsidiaries and networks. They pursue a global strategy and are controlled from their headquarters.

Features: huge capital resources (and ability to raise funds from many sources); foreign collaboration (agreements on technology, brands and patents with local firms); advanced technology; product innovation (strong research and development); marketing strategies (aggressive and effective, building global brands); expansion of market territory (operations spread across borders); centralised control (headquarters in the home country controls the branches and subsidiaries).
MNCs bring investment, technology and jobs to host countries, but they can also outcompete local firms because of their size.

example.q: A carmaker headquartered in Japan has plants in India, Thailand and Mexico, all following product and pricing policies set by the head office. Which feature of global enterprises does this show?
steps: Operations in many countries = expansion of market territory.
Policies decided by the head office = centralised control.
example.answer: Expansion of market territory with centralised control by headquarters.

learn.reallife: Maruti Suzuki is a well-known example of foreign collaboration: Suzuki of Japan brought technology and design to an Indian partner.

learn.hook: Many new highways and airport terminals in India were built neither by the government alone nor by a private company alone, but by both together.
points: Joint venture (JV): two or more independent firms pool resources and expertise for a common purpose, usually forming a new entity. Partners share ownership, control, profits and risks.

Benefits of JVs: increased resources and capacity; access to new markets and distribution networks; access to technology; innovation; low cost of production (e.g. using local labour and materials); established brand name of a partner.

Public-private partnership (PPP): a model in which tasks, obligations and risks are allocated between public and private partners in an optimal way. The government provides support such as land, policy and funding; the private partner brings capital, expertise and efficient operations.

Features of PPP: used in sectors such as power, roads, ports, airports, water and sanitation, hospitals and schools; government handles social obligations and regulation, private partner is responsible for efficiency; revenue or profits are shared as agreed.

example.q: An Indian company with a strong rural distribution network partners with a foreign company that has advanced battery technology to make electric scooters. What benefits does each gain?
steps: Indian partner gains access to technology and innovation.
Foreign partner gains access to new markets and an established distribution network.
Both share resources, costs and risks.
example.answer: Indian firm: technology; foreign firm: market access and distribution; both: shared resources and risk.

learn.reallife: Several Indian airports and expressways are developed under PPP, where the government provides land and approvals while private developers build and operate them.
